title: How to Run a Heuristic Evaluation of a Website
text:
A heuristic evaluation is a quick way to find usability problems by reviewing a website against a set of established design principles. It is a good first step in a redesign because it needs no participants and can be done in a few hours.
This article uses the redesign of Flame Kabob, a Persian restaurant website in Las Vegas, as an example.

title: How to Run a Heuristic Evaluation of a Website
text:
Before you start
You need:

The website you want to review
A list of heuristics. Most teams use Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics.
A spreadsheet to record problems

title: How to Run a Heuristic Evaluation of a Website
text:
Steps

List the key tasks. Write down the few things users most need to do on the site. For a restaurant, this is usually viewing the menu, checking hours and location, and placing an order.
Walk through each task. Complete each task yourself and note every point where you hesitate, get lost, or make a mistake.
Match each problem to a heuristic. Record which principle the problem breaks. This keeps your findings objective and easy to explain to others.
Rate the severity. Use a scale from 0 (not a problem) to 4 (prevents users from finishing a task), so the team knows what to fix first.
Summarize the findings. Group similar problems and list the most severe ones at the top.




The original Flame Kabob homepage, with inconsistent fonts and colors and unclear navigation icons.

title: How to Run a Heuristic Evaluation of a Website
text:
Example findings
The Flame Kabob evaluation found these problems:







Problem
Heuristic broken




Homepage styles were visually inconsistent
Consistency and standards


The menu was not interactive
Flexibility and efficiency of use


Navigation icons were poorly prioritized
Aesthetic and minimalist design


Colors and fonts did not match the brand
Aesthetic and minimalist design

title: How to Run a Heuristic Evaluation of a Website
text:
Tips

Have two or three people evaluate separately, then combine the lists. One evaluator usually misses many problems.
A heuristic evaluation does not replace real users. Follow it with interviews or usability testing, as the Flame Kabob team did with 12 user interviews.

title: How to Run a Closed Card Sort
text:
A closed card sort shows you how users expect content to be grouped on a website. Participants sort a set of cards (such as product names) into categories that you have already defined. The results tell you whether your navigation labels and structure match how people think.
This article uses the Natural Beauty project, a website and app for a vegan cosmetics brand, as an example.

title: How to Run a Closed Card Sort
text:
Closed or open?

In a closed card sort, you provide the categories. Use it to test a structure you already have.
In an open card sort, participants create their own categories. Use it early, when you have no structure yet.

title: How to Run a Closed Card Sort
text:
Before you start
You need:

A draft list of categories (your main navigation)
20 to 40 cards, each showing one piece of content, such as a product type
Participants who match your target users
Physical cards or an online tool such as Optimal Workshop

title: How to Run a Closed Card Sort
text:
Steps

Write the cards. Use plain words that users would recognize, and avoid copying your category names onto the cards, since that makes the answers obvious.
Set up the categories. Place them where every participant can see them.
Run the sessions. Ask each participant to place every card in the category where they would expect to find it. Ask them to think aloud so you hear their reasoning.
Record the results. Note where each card was placed and any cards that participants hesitated over.
Look for patterns. Cards placed in the same category by most participants confirm your structure. Cards that were spread across several categories point to confusing labels.
Update your site map. Rename or move categories based on what you learned.




The Natural Beauty site map, organized by product category after the card sort sessions.

title: How to Run a Closed Card Sort
text:
Example
The Natural Beauty team ran five closed card sorting sessions. The results shaped the site map and confirmed how users expected to move between product categories before any wireframes were drawn.

title: How to Run a Closed Card Sort
text:
Tips

Five sessions can reveal clear patterns on a small site. Larger sites usually need more participants.
Card sorting tests structure, not visual design. Test the finished navigation later with usability testing.

title: UX Methods Guide
text: This site explains three UX research methods that help teams find problems, organize content, and test designs. Each guide gives you the steps to run the method yourself and shows a real project as an example.

title: UX Methods Guide
text:
Guides

How to Run a Heuristic Evaluation of a Website

Review a website against established usability principles to find problems before a redesign. Example: Flame Kabob restaurant website.

How to Run a Closed Card Sort

Test whether your site’s categories match how users expect content to be grouped. Example: Natural Beauty cosmetics website and app.

How to Run a Usability Test and Score It with SUS

Compare two designs using real tasks, error counts, and a standard satisfaction score. Example: Parks Library study room booking redesign.

title: UX Methods Guide
text:
Who this is for
These guides are for students and beginners in UX design who want a quick, practical starting point. No special software is needed.

title: How to Run a Usability Test and Score It with SUS
text:
title: “How to Run a Usability Test and Score It with SUS” description: “Compare two designs using tasks, error counts, and a standard satisfaction score.” —
A usability test shows how well real people can complete tasks with a design. Adding the System Usability Scale (SUS), a short standard questionnaire, gives you a single score you can compare against other designs.
This article uses the Parks Library study room booking redesign at Iowa State University as an example.

title: How to Run a Usability Test and Score It with SUS
text:
Before you start
You need:

The designs you want to test, such as the current system and a prototype
Three to five realistic tasks
Participants who match your target users
A way to record time, errors, and task completion
The SUS questionnaire (10 questions, each answered on a 1 to 5 scale)

title: How to Run a Usability Test and Score It with SUS
text:
Steps

Write the tasks. Each task should have a clear goal and end point, such as “Book a room for four people tomorrow at 2 p.m.”
Choose a study design. In a within-subjects study, each participant uses both designs. Switch which design goes first for half the participants, so learning does not affect the results.
Run the sessions. Give one task at a time. Do not help participants unless they are completely stuck.
Measure performance. Record completion time, number of errors, and whether each task was completed.
Give the SUS questionnaire. Participants fill it out after using each design.
Calculate the SUS score for each participant, then average the scores.

title: How to Run a Usability Test and Score It with SUS
text:
Calculating SUS
Odd questions (1, 3, 5, 7, 9):   response - 1
Even questions (2, 4, 6, 8, 10): 5 - response
SUS score = (sum of all 10 values) x 2.5
Scores range from 0 to 100. The average score across many studies is 68, so a score above 68 is above average.



The redesigned booking screen, showing the drag-to-select timeline and room details side panel.
